By this judgment, this Court shall decide the suit of Mrs. Neelam Gandhi (hereinafter referred to as 'plaintiff') against National Insurance Company Limited (hereinafter referred to as 'defendant')
for damages/mesne profits of .6,69,587.22 w.e.f. 01.5.2010 to 31.10.2010 at the rate of .1,11,597.87 per month in respect of the suit property alongwith pendent-lite and future interest @12% per annum till realization and for future damages/mesne profits during the pendency of the present suit w.e.f. 01.11.2010 to 17.05.2013 @1,67,200/- per month when the possession was handed over to the plaintiff alongwith pendent- lite and future interest @12% per annum till realisation.
PLEADINGS Brief Facts pleaded in the plaint 2.

It is the case of the plaintiff that on 03.10.2008, the plaintiff through sale deed bought the property bearing no. No.2281, First Floor, Gali No. 17, Plot No. 117, Ward No.XVI, Hardhian Singh Road, Beadon Pura, Karol Bagh, New Delhi- 110005 measuring 1520 Sq.ft from Smt. Nita Gill, in which defendant was the tenant through a registered lease deed for nine years and was paying rent of .55602.13 per month exclusive of electricity and water charges for business purposes.

3. sentences.text: Then, despite service of legal notice sent by the plaintiff dated 05.04.2010 as per the mandate of Section 106 of Transfer of property Act, defendant did not vacate the property.

4. It is averred by the plaintiff that since the actual market rate of rent of similar premises in the area is about @.110/- per sq. ft. and as such the market rate of rent of area 1520 sq. ft comes to .1,67,200/- per month and as such defendant is liable to pay the damages @.1,67,200/- per month.
The defendant has been paying occupation charges to the plaintiff @.55,602.13/- only even after expiry of lease and termination of lease by notice.

The plaintiff is claiming damages @.1,67,200/- per month w.e.f. 01.05.2010 and the defendant has paid .55,602.13 only to the plaintiff even after termination of the tenancy and as such defendant is liable to pay the difference of the amount of .1,11,597.87 (market rate which is .1,67,200/- less the amount paid .55,602.13)
w.e.f. 01.05.2010 to 31.10.2010, total amounting of .6,69,587.22 and further @.1,67,200/- per month till 17.05.2013 when the possession of the suit property was handed over to the plaintiff

.

23. None of the plaintiff witnesses filed or produced any document to prove the contentions of the plaint and their respective affidavits regarding the rate of rent.
In the absence of any documentary proof or supportive evidence the claim of the plaintiff cannot be admitted merely on the basis of the bald averments.
It is an admitted position of fact that the last paid rent was of .55,602.13/- per month.

PW3 brought a lease deed Ex PW3/1 (OSR) of a property of Karol Bagh area where the suit property is situated the rate of rent was shown as . 1,25,000 per month for the area measuring as 183 sq ft on the ground floor and 330 sq ft. on the basement, that comes to

around  243/- per sq ft.
24.
Besides oral averments only PW3/1 (OSR) is a document on which plaintiff heavily relied upon to substantiate its claim of rate of rent.
However, PW3 himself deposed that he has no knowledge about the distance between the suit property and property which is the subject matter of PW3/1 (OSR).

Though, it is not the actual situation but even if this Court assumes that both the properties are situated in the same vicinity then only the location cannot be sole factor to determine the rate of rent.
Because the floor, amenities, ambiance, view, accessibility, purpose, condition, quality of construction etc. are the major SANDEEP

Therefore, in the absence of the information about the facts of the property as mentioned in PW3/1 (OSR) it cannot be considered as a lighting factor to determine the rate of rent in the present matter.

25. In nutshell, neither the plaintiff's has produced anything on record to substantiate the amount of rent as claimed  110/- per sq.ft nor by the defendant to prove that it was around  39/- per sq. ft.
At this juncture it would be appropriate to refer to Section 2(12) of the CPC, which defines mesne profits and upon which provision the claim of the plaintiff is premised.

The provision reads as under:-
"2 Definitions

In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context, xxxxxxx (12) "mesne profits" of property means those profits which the person in wrongful possession of such property actually received or might with ordinary diligence have received therefrom, together with interest on such profits,
but shall not include profits due to improvements made by the person in wrongful possession;"
26.

A bare perusal of the section 2 (12) CPC, which defines mesne profits, makes it clear that mesne profits are those profits which a landlord is entitled to get from a tenant, who continues to occupy the tenanted property even after the tenancy has ended and are defined as the amount of rent that would have otherwise been collected on a tenanted property during the time when tenant was occupying it illegally/without authority.

However, figuring out how much should be paid to the owner or landlord in SANDEEP SANDEEP KUMAR KUMAR SHARMA Date: 2024.04.19 Judgment Neelam Gandhi vs National Insurance Co. Ltd on 12 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/127773150/

sentences.text: relation to these mesne profits is a burden that the courts frequently bear.
This process of determination of mesne profits begins with the landlord discharging the onus placed upon him to prove his claim for mesne profits in accordance with the law.
After that, the appropriate mesne profits to be awarded by the Court by appreciating the evidence or making further enquiry, if required.

27. Now adverting to the facts of the present case, it is observed that the tenancy in respect of the suit property stood duly terminated through a legal notice Ex PW1/4 dated 05.04.2010 and the occupation of the suit property by the defendants after 05.4.2010 become wrongful and without any plaintiff's authority and made entitled to plaintiff to the mesne profits/damages from the defendants for being in wrongful use and occupation of the suit property.
The said mesne profits would obviously be the prevailing market rent of the suit property at the time when the occupation of the defendants becomes contumacious.

To prove the prevailing market rent of the suit property at the relevant time i.e. when the tenancy was terminated, it was incumbent upon the plaintiff to lead evidence to prove the rental value of the properties in the vicinity of the suit property or to bring forth any other positive evidence to substantiate their claim of mesne profits @  1,67,200/- per month for the period from 1.05.2010 to 17.05.2013.
28.

As already stated earlier that barring simple statements in evidence none of the PWs brought any other substantial evidence SANDEEP Digitally by SANDEEP signed KUMAR KUMAR SHARMA Date: 2024.04.19 SHARMA 11:59:35 +0530 Judgment dt. 12.04.2024 CS DJ No. 11035/2016 Neelam Gandhi Vs. National Insurance Company Limited Page No. 13 of 22 to prove the prevailing market rent of which the suit property was capable of being let out at the relevant time.

sentences.text:
However,
just because the plaintiff failed to prove the prevailing market rate, this does not in any way limit the jurisdiction of the court to award reasonable mesne profits/damages and it is well established that in the absence of any direct evidence that could assist the court in determining the reasonable amount, the court may exercise its judicial discretion to estimate the amount of mesne profits in order to do justice and some amount of guess work is always involved in determining the mesne profits/damages.
It is trite, that the exercise of this judicial discretion should not be arbitrary and must confirm to sound judicial principles.

In the case in hand because no direct evidence was led by plaintiff in the form of a lease deed or any other document evidencing the rental value for any comparable properties in the vicinity of the suit property at the relevant time, which could have assisted this Court in determining the amount of mesne profits, therefore, this Court may exercise its judicial discretion to assess the amount of mesne profits.

29. To exercise its discretion this Court is drawing strength from the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi where in case titled as 'M/s. M.C. Agarwal HUF vs. M/s. Sahara India & Ors.2011 (183) DLT 105' it was held that to arrive at the conclusion that there has been general increase in the rental value of the properties in the urban areas and judicial notice of the said fact could be taken without there being any formal proof of the same by the party who is obliged to prove the same and by way SANDEEP

We find that this Court has in several cases taken judicial notice of the factum of increase of rent and made awards of mesne profits and damages.
Noteworthy in this behalf is a judicial pronouncement of the Division Bench reported at (supra) entitled Vinod Kumar v. Bakshi Sachdev.
This judgment was delivered by a Division Bench of which one of us (Dr. M.K. Sharma, J.) had delivered the judgment.

"21.

The learned Counsel for the appellants also urged before us that the learned Trial Court was not justified in taking a judicial notice of the fact of increase of rents like the suit property and also in providing Rs. 10,000/- per month as fair amount towards damages/mesne profits in favor of the plaintiff.
It is true that no substantial evidence has been led by the plaintiff in respect of the increase of rent in the properties like that of the suit property.

However, it is a well known fact that the amount of rent for various properties in and around Delhi has been rising staggeringly and we cannot see why such judicial notice could not be taken of the fact about such increase of rents in the premises in and around Delhi which is a city of growing importance being the capital of the country which is a matter of public history.

A bare perusal of the section 2 (12) CPC, which defines mesne profits, makes it clear that mesne profits are those profits which a landlord is entitled to get from a tenant, who continues to occupy the tenanted property even after the tenancy has ended and are defined as the amount of rent that would have otherwise been collected on a tenanted property during the time when tenant was occupying it illegally/without authority.
relation to these mesne profits is a burden that the courts frequently bear.
This process of determination of mesne profits begins with the landlord discharging the onus placed upon him to prove his claim for mesne profits in accordance with the law.
After that, the appropriate mesne profits to be awarded by the Court by appreciating the evidence or making further enquiry, if required.
To prove the prevailing market rent of the suit property at the relevant time i.e. when the tenancy was terminated, it was incumbent upon the plaintiff to lead evidence to prove the rental value of the properties in the vicinity of the suit property or to bring forth any other positive evidence to substantiate their claim of mesne profits @  1,67,200/- per month for the period from 1.05.2010 to 17.05.2013.
28.
However,
just because the plaintiff failed to prove the prevailing market rate, this does not in any way limit the jurisdiction of the court to award reasonable mesne profits/damages and it is well established that in the absence of any direct evidence that could assist the court in determining the reasonable amount, the court may exercise its judicial discretion to estimate the amount of mesne profits in order to do justice and some amount of guess work is always involved in determining the mesne profits/damages.
It is trite, that the exercise of this judicial discretion should not be arbitrary and must confirm to sound judicial principles.
In the case in hand because no direct evidence was led by plaintiff in the form of a lease deed or any other document evidencing the rental value for any comparable properties in the vicinity of the suit property at the relevant time, which could have assisted this Court in determining the amount of mesne profits, therefore, this Court may exercise its judicial discretion to assess the amount of mesne profits.
